title: What is lock fairness in ReentrantLock, how does a fair (FIFO) lock prevent starvation, and what is the throughput trade-off of fair versus unfair mode?
shortTitle: Lock fairness — FIFO prevents starvation but reduces throughput

s1_definition.profdef: `ReentrantLock` can be constructed in fair or unfair mode. A fair lock grants ownership in first-in-first-out order of the threads that requested it, so the longest-waiting thread acquires the lock next, which prevents starvation. An unfair lock (the default) allows barging: when the lock is released, any thread, including one that just arrived, may grab it ahead of threads already queued, which increases throughput because it avoids the overhead of handing off to a parked thread, at the cost that an unlucky thread could wait a long time. Fairness guarantees ordering but reduces throughput; unfairness maximizes throughput but allows temporary unfairness.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India there is one cash counter. A fair lock is a strict token queue: customers take a numbered token and are served in exact order, so nobody is skipped, but every handover involves calling the next token holder, who may be sitting far away, which wastes a few seconds each time. An unfair lock is a free-for-all at the counter: the moment the teller is free, whoever is standing closest jumps in, even if someone has been waiting longer. The free-for-all serves more customers per hour because there is no delay waking a distant person, but an unlucky customer at the back could wait a very long time.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fair locks serve threads in FIFO order to prevent starvation but pay a wake-up cost that lowers throughput; unfair locks let threads barge in for higher throughput at the risk of long waits.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `ReentrantLock` can be constructed in fair or unfair mode. A fair lock grants ownership in first-in-first-out order of the threads that requested it, so the longest-waiting thread acquires the lock next, which prevents starvation. An unfair lock (the default) allows barging: when the lock is released, any thread, including one that just arrived, may grab it ahead of threads already queued, which increases throughput because it avoids the overhead of handing off to a parked thread, at the cost that an unlucky thread could wait a long time. Fairness guarantees ordering but reduces throughput; unfairness maximizes throughput but allows temporary unfairness.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India there is one cash counter. A fair lock is a strict token queue: customers take a numbered token and are served in exact order, so nobody is skipped, but every handover involves calling the next token holder, who may be sitting far away, which wastes a few seconds each time. An unfair lock is a free-for-all at the counter: the moment the teller is free, whoever is standing closest jumps in, even if someone has been waiting longer. The free-for-all serves more customers per hour because there is no delay waking a distant person, but an unlucky customer at the back could wait a very long time.

**One line to remember:** Fair locks serve threads in FIFO order to prevent starvation but pay a wake-up cost that lowers throughput; unfair locks let threads barge in for higher throughput at the risk of long waits.

sections.s2_technical:
You choose the mode in the constructor: `new ReentrantLock()` is unfair, and `new ReentrantLock(true)` is fair. Everything else about the API is identical — `lock()`, `unlock()`, `tryLock()`, `lockInterruptibly()`.

In fair mode, when a thread calls `lock()` and the lock is held, it joins the tail of a FIFO queue, and when the lock frees, the thread at the head is granted it. A new thread calling `lock()` will not jump the queue even if the lock is momentarily free while a handoff is in progress; it checks whether predecessors are waiting and, if so, queues behind them.

```java
ReentrantLock fair = new ReentrantLock(true);   // FIFO, no starvation
fair.lock();
try { account.debit(amount); } finally { fair.unlock(); }
```

In unfair mode, when the lock is released a newly arriving thread may grab it immediately through barging, before the queued threads are even woken. This is faster because waking a parked thread costs a context switch, and if an incoming thread can take and release the lock in that same window, overall throughput rises.

```java
ReentrantLock unfair = new ReentrantLock();     // default, high throughput
unfair.lock();
try { counter++; } finally { unfair.unlock(); }
```

One important subtlety: `tryLock()` with no timeout always barges even on a fair lock, because it is defined to grab the lock if it is free at that instant regardless of the queue. If you want tryLock to respect fairness, use the timed `tryLock(timeout, unit)`, which honors the FIFO order.

The trade-off in numbers: unfair locks typically deliver markedly higher throughput under contention because they minimize thread suspension and resumption. Fair locks sacrifice some of that throughput to guarantee that no thread waits indefinitely. So I default to unfair for maximum performance and only switch to fair when starvation is a real, observed problem — for example, when a low-priority background thread must never be perpetually starved by a storm of high-frequency threads. `synchronized` is always unfair, so when fairness truly matters, ReentrantLock in fair mode is the tool.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has a single shared end-of-day ledger lock. During peak load, dozens of fast transaction threads hammer the lock, while one slow audit thread also needs it occasionally. With the default unfair lock, the fast threads keep barging in and the audit thread can be starved for a long time, so the audit falls behind and compliance reports are late. This is exactly what a fair lock fixes: in FIFO mode, once the audit thread is queued, it is guaranteed to be served in its turn, preventing starvation.

Problem 2 — The operations team measured that switching the main transaction path to a fair lock dropped throughput noticeably because of the wake-up overhead on every handoff. So the decision is nuanced: use a fair lock only where starvation is the real risk, and keep the default unfair lock on the high-throughput hot path.

The code builds an `Account` protected by a configurable ReentrantLock, a `TransactionWorker` representing fast high-frequency threads, an `AuditWorker` representing the slow starvation-prone thread, and a demo that runs both under fair and unfair modes and reports how often the audit thread got served.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: one shared Account lock, 8 fast transaction threads that debit Rs.1 in a tight loop, and 1 slow audit thread that needs the same lock, run for 500 ms in each mode.

Step 1 (unfair mode): All 9 threads contend for the lock. When a transaction thread releases the lock, another arriving transaction thread barges in before the audit thread (which may be parked) is even woken. The audit thread rarely wins the race, so `auditServed` stays very low — this is starvation.

Step 2: The demo interrupts all threads after 500 ms and logs the unfair audit count, typically a small number because the audit thread kept losing the barging race.

Step 3 (fair mode): The same 9 threads contend, but now the lock maintains a FIFO queue. When the audit thread calls `lock()`, it joins the queue, and transaction threads arriving afterward cannot jump ahead of it. On the next release, the audit thread at the head is granted the lock.

Step 4: Each handoff in fair mode wakes the specific queued head thread, which costs a context switch, so total operations across all threads are fewer than in unfair mode — lower throughput.

Step 5: The demo logs the fair audit count, which is substantially higher than the unfair count, proving fairness prevented starvation, while total throughput was lower. The balance remains non-negative in both runs.

```
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: === mode: UNFAIR ===
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: audit served 3 times (UNFAIR)
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: === mode: FAIR ===
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: audit served 1200 times (FAIR)
```

```
  throughput: HIGH                 throughput: LOWER
    │                                 │
    └─────────────┬───────────────────┘
                  ▼
   Decision: unfair on hot path, fair only where starvation is real
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Lock fairness is a mode you choose when you construct a ReentrantLock. If I pass true to the constructor I get a fair lock, and if I use the default constructor I get an unfair lock. A fair lock grants ownership in strict first-in-first-out order, so the thread that has been waiting the longest is always served next. An unfair lock allows barging, which means when the lock is released, a thread that just arrived can grab it immediately, even ahead of threads that were already queued.

The reason fairness exists is to prevent starvation. Without it, if you have a storm of high-frequency threads constantly contending for a lock and one occasional low-frequency thread that also needs it, the fast threads keep barging in and the slow thread can be starved for a very long time. In fair mode, once that slow thread joins the queue, no later arrival can jump ahead of it, so it is guaranteed to be served in its turn.

The trade-off is throughput. Every fair handoff has to wake up the specific thread at the head of the queue, and waking a parked thread costs a context switch. An unfair lock avoids that cost because an already-running thread can barge in and finish its work in the same window, so under contention the unfair lock delivers noticeably higher throughput. That is why unfair is the default, and why synchronized is always unfair. One subtlety I mention is that tryLock with no timeout always barges even on a fair lock, so if I want tryLock to respect fairness I have to use the timed version.

At National Bank of India we had a shared ledger lock where fast transaction threads were starving a slow audit thread, and compliance reports were falling behind. We measured it: under the default unfair lock the audit thread was served only a handful of times, but when we switched that specific path to a fair lock the audit thread was served consistently, at the cost of lower overall throughput. So the decision we landed on was to keep the default unfair lock on the high-throughput transaction hot path and use a fair lock only where starvation was a real, observed problem. The sentence I give interviewers is that fair locks trade throughput for ordering to prevent starvation, unfair locks trade ordering for throughput, and I default to unfair and reach for fair only when a thread is genuinely being starved.
